title: Why Your New Car Loses Thousands the Moment You Drive Home
description:
The moment a new car rolls off the dealer lot, its value drops by thousands, even though nothing about the car has changed. Using a stickman detective, this video explains where that money goes: depreciation is the biggest cost of owning a new car (AAA 2026: about $4,422 of $12,863 a year), and George Akerlof's Nobel-winning "Market for Lemons" explains why value falls before the car has done anything at all. We also look at what stretching a loan to 84 months does to total interest.

In this video:
- Hook: the price tag that drops at the gate
- The mystery: a record $51,109 average new-car price
- Wrong guess #1: the dealer kept it
- Wrong guess #2: the car got worse
- Clue #1: the biggest cost of owning a car isn't gas, it's depreciation
- Clue #2: what does the next buyer know?
- The answer: Akerlof's market for lemons (2001 Nobel Prize)
- Back to the crime scene: the price of missing information
- Bonus clue: the 84-month loan calendar
- The daily view: about $35.24 a day
- What this means for you: three ideas worth keeping
- Wrap-up
